solution:
| States /Regions | India | Brazil |
|---|---|---|
| High rainfall | Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayas, West Bengal, Goa | Amazonas, Roraima |
| Moderate rainfall | Bihar, Eastern Maharastra | Tocantins, Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina |
| Low rainfall | Western part of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Western Andhra Pradesh | Pernambuco, Alagoas, Rio Grande Do Norte, Paraiba |

The grouping follows what the chapter says about rainfall in the two countries.

In India the moisture-laden monsoon winds are obstructed by the Eastern and Western Ghats, so it rains more in the coastal areas and less on the leeward side of the hills; the winds blow parallel to the Aravalis, so rainfall is low in parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan; and orographic rainfall occurs at the Himalayas. The chapter also names Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in Meghalaya, in the eastern Himalayan region, as the wettest places in the world, and Jaisalmer in western Rajasthan as the driest part of India, receiving less than 120 mm a year.

In Brazil the Amazon valley receives around 2000 mm of rainfall while the north-eastern coast receives only 1000 to 1200 mm. The escarpment blocks the winds blowing from the sea, and beyond the highlands their effect is reduced, so the north-eastern part is a rain-shadow region called the 'Drought Quadrilateral' — the states of Pernambuco, Alagoas, Rio Grande do Norte and Paraiba lie in it.

[Note: the printed word bank lists 'Roroima' and 'Roraima', which appear to be the same Brazilian state printed twice.]

Right.

The equator passes through the northern part of Brazil, and the chapter says the temperature is more in that region. Most of the country lies in the tropical zone, and near the equator it is hot while a temperate type of climate is found near the Tropic of Capricorn — so the country's whole range of climate follows from where the equator crosses it.

The equator also explains why Brazil has almost no tropical cyclones: in the coastal regions near it the differences in temperature are negligible, the winds move vertically and the convergence zone of the trade winds is weak, so cyclones are not formed.

Wrong.

Corrected sentence: India and Brazil have opposite seasons at the same time.

India lies wholly in the northern hemisphere, while most of Brazil lies in the southern hemisphere. The two are therefore tilted towards the sun at opposite times of the year, so when it is summer in India it is winter in most of Brazil and the other way round.

Right.

The chapter says that India faces natural disasters like erratic rainfall, droughts, cyclones and floods frequently. India has a long coastline on the Indian Ocean, and the conditions that Brazil lacks — a strong convergence of winds rather than vertical movement near the equator — are present here, so tropical cyclones do strike India often.

Wrong.

Corrected sentence: Brazil gets a lot of rainfall because of the South-East Trade winds and the North-East Trade winds.

The chapter states this directly: Brazil gets rainfall from the South-East Trade winds and the North-East Trade Winds. The south-west monsoon winds are the rain-bearing winds of India, not of Brazil; they form because high temperatures in summer create a low pressure area in the Punjab plains and the Thar desert, which draws in moist winds from the Indian Ocean.

Parts of the Brazilian highlands extend up to the northern coast, and the escarpments act as an obstruction to the winds blowing from the sea. Those winds are forced to rise over the escarpment and give orographic rainfall in the coastal region.

Beyond the highlands the effect of these winds is reduced, because they have already shed their moisture on the seaward side. As a result the rainfall there is minimal.

The north-eastern part of the Brazilian Highlands is therefore a rain-shadow region, and the chapter calls it the 'Drought Quadrilateral'.

Brazil is a tropical country. Most of it lies in the tropical zone, the equator passes through its northern part, and its temperatures are high, so it normally does not receive snowfall at all.

Snow falls there only in exceptional conditions, when southern polar air masses reach the southern part of Brazil. Because that happens rarely, snowfall does not always occur — the chapter records it in only three years, 1879, 1957 and 1985.

Convectional rainfall occurs where the air is heated strongly at one place, rises vertically and cools, and where that happens day after day through the year.

India's rainfall is not made that way. The chapter says India's climate is of the 'monsoon' type: high summer temperatures create a low pressure area in the Punjab plains and the Thar desert of Rajasthan, which draws in moisture-laden winds from the high pressure region over the Indian Ocean. Where those winds meet the Eastern and Western Ghats and later the Himalayas they are forced to rise, so India's rain is largely orographic, and it falls in a definite rainy season rather than throughout the year.

Brazil is where the vertical movement of air near the equator is described in this chapter, so it is there rather than in India that convectional conditions prevail.

In the coastal regions of Brazil near the equator the differences in temperature are negligible.

Because of this, the winds there move in the vertical direction, and the convergence zone of the trade winds is weak in this region.

A tropical cyclone needs winds converging strongly at the surface. Since that convergence is weak here, cyclones are not formed, and so tropical cyclones rarely visit the coasts of Brazil.

Manaus lies in the Amazon valley, close to the equator, in the northern part of Brazil.

The chapter says that near the equator at the Brazilian coast the temperature does not vary much and that in the coastal regions near the equator the differences in temperature are negligible. The sun's rays fall almost vertically there throughout the year, so there is little seasonal change, and the average temperature in the Amazon valley stays between 25° and 28° C.

Because the temperature stays near that level all year, the range of temperature at Manaus is small.

The south-west monsoon winds, after bringing rain to most of India, reach the Himalayas and are turned back.

The chapter says these winds return from the Himalayan ranges and their retreating journey starts. While blowing from the north-east towards the Indian Ocean they bring rainfall again to some parts of the Peninsula. This is the Retreating Monsoon season, one of the four seasons recognised by the Indian Meteorological Department.

So India receives precipitation from the North-East Monsoon winds as well as from the south-west ones. The chapter adds that Tamil Nadu receives its maximum rainfall during the retreating monsoon season.

The Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of India, so India is considered to be in the tropical region and its climate is of the 'monsoon' type.

Temperature: the sun's rays are perpendicular up to the Tropic of Cancer, so average temperatures are high throughout the year, and they increase towards the south. Going northwards they fall, until in winter the temperature drops to −40° Celsius in Jammu and Kashmir and parts of the mountainous regions of the Himalayas. The chapter notes both extremes: Ganganagar in Rajasthan reaches 50° C in June, while Kargil often experiences −48° C in winter.

Rainfall: the moisture-laden winds from the Indian Ocean are obstructed by the Eastern and Western Ghats, so it rains more in the coastal areas of the south and less on the leeward side. Further north the winds blow parallel to the Aravalis, so rainfall is low in parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Still further north their moisture-carrying capacity increases and the Himalayas force them to rise, giving orographic rainfall — Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in Meghalaya are the wettest places in the world.

So going from south to north the climate changes from hot and, on the coasts, wet, through the drier interior and the desert of the north-west, to the very cold and snowy mountain climate of the far north.

The chapter says that the Indian Ocean and the Himalayan ranges exert a great influence on the climate of India and on the origin of the monsoons.

The Himalayas act first as a wall. Very cold winds blowing from the north are obstructed by them, which is why India stays hot throughout the year instead of being as cold as places at the same latitude beyond the mountains. They act second as a barrier that makes rain: when the monsoon winds reach them their moisture-carrying capacity has increased, and the natural obstruction of the Himalayas forces them to rise, giving orographic rainfall. Third, they turn the winds back — the South-West Monsoons retreat from the Shiwalik and Himachal ranges, and that retreat begins the Retreating Monsoon season.

The Indian Ocean is the source of the moisture. Because of high summer temperatures a low pressure area develops in the Punjab plains and the Thar desert of Rajasthan, and this attracts winds from the high pressure region over the Indian Ocean, which begin blowing towards the mainland. These moisture-laden winds bring the rainfall on which the country depends.

Without the ocean there would be no moisture, and without the Himalayas neither the shelter from the northern cold nor the obstruction that turns that moisture into rain.

Latitudinal extent: because of the vast latitudinal extent of Brazil it experiences a wide range of variation in climate. Near the equator it is hot, while a temperate type of climate is found near the Tropic of Capricorn. Most of the country lies in the tropical zone and the equator passes through its northern part, so the northern part is hot while temperatures in the southern part are comparatively lower.

Winds: Brazil gets its rainfall from the South-East Trade winds and the North-East Trade winds.

Relief: parts of the Brazilian highlands extend up to the northern coast, and the escarpments obstruct the winds blowing from the sea, causing orographic rainfall in the coastal region. Beyond the highlands the effect of those winds is reduced and rainfall is minimal, producing the rain-shadow region called the 'Drought Quadrilateral'. Altitude also cools the highlands.

Distance from the sea: because of its proximity to the sea the coast experiences a mild and humid climate, and near the equator at the Brazilian coast the temperature does not vary much.

The result is that the average temperature in the Amazon valley is 25°–28° C, the climate is cooler in the highlands, the Amazon valley receives around 2000 mm of rainfall and the north-eastern coast only 1000 to 1200 mm.

Both countries lie largely in the tropical zone — the Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of India and the equator through the northern part of Brazil — so both are hot for most of the year and both have a wide range of climate because of their large latitudinal extent.

They differ in almost everything else.

Type of climate: India's climate is of the 'monsoon' type, with four seasons recognised by the Indian Meteorological Department — the hot weather season, the season of rainfall, the season of retreating monsoon and the cold weather season. Brazil has no monsoon; it is hot near the equator and temperate near the Tropic of Capricorn.

Rain-bearing winds: India's rain comes from the monsoon winds drawn in from the Indian Ocean by the low pressure that develops over the Punjab plains and the Thar desert, and again from the retreating North-East monsoon. Brazil's rain comes from the South-East and North-East Trade winds.

Seasons: because India is in the northern hemisphere and most of Brazil in the southern, their seasons fall at opposite times of the year.

Extremes: India's temperatures range from 50° C at Ganganagar in June to −48° C at Kargil in winter, and it faces erratic rainfall, droughts, cyclones and floods frequently. Brazil's range is far narrower — the Amazon valley stays at 25°–28° C, tropical cyclones rarely visit its coasts, and snow falls only in exceptional years when southern polar air reaches the south.

Both, however, have a dry rain-shadow region: the 'Drought Quadrilateral' behind the Brazilian escarpment, and the lee of the Ghats and the Aravali-parallel belt of Gujarat and Rajasthan in India.

Brasilia and Bhopal are both inland cities, far from the moderating influence of the sea, so both should show a continental type of climate — a larger range between the hottest and the coldest month than a coastal city at the same latitude.

The expected difference between them follows from the hemispheres they lie in. Bhopal is in India, north of the equator, so its temperature curve should peak in the hot weather season, just before the monsoon breaks, and fall to its lowest in the cold weather season. Brasilia is in Brazil, south of the equator, so its curve should run the opposite way, because the two countries have their seasons at opposite times of the year. Brasilia also stands on the Brazilian Highlands, and the chapter says the climate is cooler in the highlands, so its temperatures should be lower than its latitude alone would suggest.

Drawn as two temperature curves on the same graph, with the months of the year along the horizontal axis and temperature in degrees Celsius up the vertical axis, the two lines should therefore be roughly mirror images of each other.

[Note: this question asks the student to obtain the actual annual average temperatures from the internet, and those figures are not given in the chapter, so the answer above gives what to expect and why rather than the values themselves.]
